modules.title: Tactics V: status examination, breakthrough, defence
modules.summary: Find tactics through a status examination of every piece, break through with pawns, and save lost positions with the defender's checklist.
modules.source: Weteschnik, Chess Tactics from Scratch ch. 11-12 (status examination, candidate moves); Steps Method Step 5 (breakthrough, draw, defending); Heisman's seeds of tactical destruction

lessons.title: Status examination
lessons.objective: Examine every piece for defects (loose, overloaded, pinned, a weak back rank) and let the defects you find name your candidate moves.

sections.md:
Weteschnik calls it the status examination. Before you hunt for a combination, take stock of the pieces. For every piece, yours and your opponent's, ask four questions:

1. What does it attack, and what does it defend?
2. Is it loose? A loose piece has no defender.
3. Is it overloaded? An overloaded piece has two jobs and can do only one of them.
4. Is it pinned, or is it the only thing that blocks a line?

Then look at both kings. Has a pawn in front of the castled king moved, or is the back rank shut in? Which squares around the king are covered?

Name the defects in short sentences: "the pawn on d4 guards c5 and blocks the d-file", "the queen is the only guard of the first rank". A combination needs defects. When two defects sit close together, the candidate moves name themselves: a double attack on two loose pieces, a deflection of an overloaded guard, a check on the back rank.

When you find no defects, stop looking for tactics and improve a piece instead.

sections.caption: Zukertort–Steinitz, World Championship 1886, Black to move. The status examination: the pawn on d4 guards c5 and it is also the only thing between the queen on d6 and the rook on d2. White's king has no luft, and nothing covers c1.

sections.prompt: Black to play. Use the defect on d4.
sections.hint: Which white pawn has two jobs? Take the thing it guards.
sections.explanation: 33...Rxc5! If 34.dxc5, the d-file opens and 34...Qxd2 wins the rook. The engine prefers 34.Rxe6, and the game went 34.Rxe6 Rc1+ 35.Nd1 Qf4!: the knight is pinned on the first rank and Steinitz won in a few moves. One pawn, two jobs: that was the defect.

sections.prompt: Black to play. Bernstein–Capablanca, Moscow 1914. Examine White's queen, the rook on c3 and the first rank, then strike.
sections.hint: The queen on e2 is the only guard of the first rank. Give it a second job.
sections.explanation: 29...Qb2!! attacks the queen and the loose rook on c3 at once. 30.Qxb2 Rd1 is mate. 30.Rc8 Qa1+ 31.Qf1 Qxf1+ 32.Kxf1 Rxc8 wins the rook, and 30.Rd3 Qb1+ 31.Qf1 Qxd3 wins it too. Every defence loses at least a rook. Bernstein resigned.

sections.question: Why can White not answer 29...Qb2 with 30.Qxb2?
options: 30...Rd1 is mate: the queen was the only guard of the first rank
The queen on e2 is pinned to the king
Black recaptures 30...Rxb2 and stays a rook up
30.Qxb2 is legal, and it wins for White
sections.explanation: The status examination found it before the move: the queen on e2 alone covered d1, e1 and f1. When it takes on b2, the rook enters on d1 with mate, because the pawns on f2, g2 and h2 take the king's squares.

lessons.title: The breakthrough
lessons.objective: Use a pawn sacrifice to make a passed pawn against an equal number of pawns, and stop the same trick when you defend.

sections.md:
Three pawns against three, all blocked, kings far away. It looks equal. It is not, when your pawns stand on the fifth rank and the enemy pawns are still on the seventh.

The breakthrough: push the middle pawn and give it away. With pawns on a5, b5 and c5 against a7, b7 and c7, White plays 1.b6!. If 1...cxb6, then 2.a6! bxa6 3.c6 and the c-pawn runs. If 1...axb6, then 2.c6! bxc6 3.a6. White gives two pawns, and the third one queens because no black pawn can reach it.

Check three things before you start. Your pawns must be close to promotion. The enemy king must be too far away to catch the new passed pawn. And the opponent must not queen first on the other wing. Count every tempo.

The defender has one resource. If it is his move, he pushes his own middle pawn first. That fixes the pawns, and every exchange leaves them blocked.

sections.prompt: White to play and win. The kings are far away.
sections.hint: Give away the middle pawn.
sections.explanation: 1.b6! If 1...cxb6 2.a6! bxa6 3.c6 and the c-pawn queens. If 1...axb6 2.c6! bxc6 3.a6 and the a-pawn queens. The kings are too far away to stop either pawn. A quiet king move such as 1.Kg1 lets Black play 1...b6 and the position is a draw.

sections.caption: The same pattern on the kingside. 1.g6! and after 1...fxg6 comes 2.h6!, after 1...hxg6 comes 2.f6!. Two pawns are given so that the third one gets through.

sections.question: White played 1.g6 and Black answered 1...hxg6. Which move wins now?
options: 2.hxg6
2.fxg6
2.Kb2
sections.explanation: 2.f6! gxf6 3.h6 and the h-pawn queens; on 2...g5 White takes 3.fxg7. 2.hxg6 fxg6 or 2.fxg6 fxg6 leaves blocked pawns and a draw. 2.Kb2 lets Black take on h5.

sections.prompt: Black to move. Stop the breakthrough before it starts.
sections.hint: Which black pawn must move so that White's middle pawn has nothing to break through?
sections.explanation: 1...g6! After 2.hxg6 hxg6 3.fxg6 fxg6 (or the captures in the other order) the pawns are blocked and the position is a draw. Any other move lets White break through: for example 1...Kb7 2.g6! and White queens.

sections.prompt: Promote a pawn within 8 moves. The black king is on h1, far from your pawns' queening squares.
sections.tip: Start with the middle pawn: 1.g6!. Answer ...fxg6 with h6 and ...hxg6 with f6. Then push the free pawn.

sections.question: Before you play a breakthrough, which of these do you NOT need to check?
options: Whether your bishop is on a good diagonal
Whether the enemy king can catch the new passed pawn
Whether the enemy can queen first on the other wing
Whether your pawns are close enough to promotion
sections.explanation: The breakthrough is a count of tempi: how fast your new passed pawn queens, whether the enemy king is inside its square, and whether the other side queens first. The bishop's diagonal does not enter the count.

lessons.title: Draws and defending
lessons.objective: When you are worse, look first for the forcing draws (perpetual check and stalemate), then for activity, before you defend passively.

sections.md:
Club players often resign too early, or they defend passively and lose slowly. Here is a short checklist for the defender. Run it every move when you are worse.

1. Perpetual check. Can my queen or rook check forever? After each check, count the king's squares.
2. Stalemate. Is my king almost without moves? Then every piece of mine that disappears brings stalemate closer.
3. Known draws: the wrong bishop, the rook's pawn, opposite-coloured bishops, Philidor's position.
4. Activity. A passive piece loses slowly. Give a pawn if it makes your rook or king active.
5. Exchange the attackers. Every attacking piece you trade makes the attack weaker.

The order matters. The forcing draws come first, because they need no judgement: the board tells you at once whether they work. Activity and exchanges come next, because they need an evaluation.

sections.prompt: White to move. Black is a rook and a bishop up and threatens your king. Save the game.
sections.hint: Find a check, then count the black king's squares after each check.
sections.explanation: 1.Qh5+! Kg8 2.Qe8+ Kh7 3.Qh5+ and the checks never stop. On h7 the king has only g8; on g8 it has only h7. No black piece can block on h6 or f8. Every other white move loses.

sections.prompt: Black to move. Queen against pawn: is there a way out?
sections.hint: One king move walks into the corner. What happens if White takes the pawn then?
sections.explanation: 1...Ka1! If 2.Qxc2, Black is stalemated. The white king is too far away to help, so the queen can only give checks, and the black king keeps returning to a1 and b1. 1...Kc1? stands in front of the pawn: White gains time with checks, brings the king and wins.

sections.prompt: White to move. Anand–Carlsen, World Championship 2013, game 6. Black's king and pawns are very active. Which move keeps the draw?
sections.hint: Passive defence of the kingside will not hold. Make your queenside pawns count.
sections.explanation: 60.b4! creates counterplay on the queenside while the rook stays active. The engine rates it about -0.5, close to a draw, and every other move -1.5 or worse. Anand played 60.Ra4? and lost after 60...h3! 61.gxh3 Rg6 62.c4 f3, and the f-pawn decided.

sections.prompt: Draw the game. Black is a rook and a bishop up and threatens mate on g2 and h2.
sections.tip: Check from e8 and h5. After each check the black king has one square.

sections.question: Black to move. Is this position a draw?
options: Yes: the bishop does not control h8, and the king cannot be driven out of the corner
No: White wins by pushing h7
No: White wins by bringing the bishop to e5
Yes, but only because it is Black's move
sections.explanation: The h-pawn queens on h8, a dark square, and the bishop on c2 runs on light squares. The black king shuffles between h8 and g8; if White pushes h7 at the wrong moment it is stalemate. This is the wrong-coloured bishop: a draw whoever moves.

modules.title: Calculation discipline: Kotov and Aagaard
modules.summary: Make a list of candidates before you calculate, calculate each line once to a quiet position, ask three questions in quiet positions, and take a last look before you move.
modules.source: Kotov, Think Like a Grandmaster (candidate moves, the tree of analysis, Blumenfeld's rule); Aagaard, Grandmaster Preparation: Calculation and Positional Play (the three questions); Yusupov, Boost Your Chess 3 ch. 9 (the technique of calculating variations)

lessons.title: Candidate moves first
lessons.objective: List every candidate move, forcing moves first, before you calculate any of them.

sections.md:
Kotov's first rule: before you calculate, make a list. Name every candidate move, then calculate them one by one. A player who calculates the first move he sees often misses the best one, which was second or third on a list he never made.

Build the list in this order:

1. Checks. They limit the reply to a few king moves or blocks.
2. Captures, including the ones that look bad.
3. Threats: moves that attack a piece or threaten mate.
4. The quiet move that improves your worst piece.

Make the same list for your opponent. His checks and captures are the moves that can refute yours.

Forcing moves come first because they keep the tree small. After a check the opponent may have two replies; after a quiet move he may have thirty. A three-move combination of checks is easier to calculate than one quiet move.

sections.caption: Rubinstein–Lasker, St Petersburg 1909. Lasker has just played 16...Rxe3. The natural recapture 17.fxe3 loses to 17...Qxg2 mate: the bishop on c6 covers g2. The list must start with the checks.

sections.prompt: White to play. Make your list: checks, captures, threats. Then calculate the check.
sections.hint: Start with the check on c6. After 17...bxc6, which queen move attacks two things?
sections.explanation: 17.Rxc6+! bxc6 18.Qc1! attacks the rook on e3 and the pawn on c6. The game went 18...Rxd4 19.fxe3 Rd7 20.Qxc6+ Kd8 21.Rf4 and White's queen and rook hunt the open king (engine about +2). Rubinstein won the ending. On 18.fxe3? Qxe3+ Black is fine. 17.fxe3?? Qxg2 is mate.

sections.question: Before you calculate anything here, list White's checks. How many are there?
options: Two: 19.Bxh7+ and 19.Qxf7+
One: 19.Bxh7+
Three: 19.Bxh7+, 19.Qxf7+ and 19.Ng5
None
sections.explanation: 19.Bxh7+ and 19.Qxf7+ are the only checks; 19.Ng5 is a threat, not a check. 19.Qxf7+? Rxf7 just loses the queen, so it is crossed off at once. 19.Bxh7+ is the one to calculate.

sections.prompt: White to play. Polugaevsky–Tal, USSR Championship 1969. Calculate the check you kept on your list.
sections.hint: A bishop check on h7 starts it. After the king takes, the knight checks. Then which pawn joins the attack?
sections.explanation: 19.Bxh7+! Kxh7 20.Ng5+ Kg6 21.h4! The h-pawn threatens h5+ and the queen and knight close in. If 20...Kg8, then 21.Qh4 threatens mate on h7. The quiet 19.Rd2 leads to exchanges and a level game.

lessons.title: The tree: calculate each line once
lessons.objective: Follow a forcing line to its end, one branch at a time, and judge the final position before you play the first move.

sections.md:
Kotov's second rule: calculate each branch of the tree once. A player who jumps between lines, a bit of this, a bit of that, back to the first, wastes time and still misses things.

The method:

1. Take your first candidate. Follow it move by move until the position is quiet: no checks, no captures, no threats left.
2. Judge that final position in one sentence: "I am a piece up", "his king is mated", "equal".
3. Only then go to the next candidate. Do not return to a line you have finished.
4. Compare the verdicts and choose.

For each of your moves, take the opponent's strongest reply first: his checks and captures. If your line survives his best answer, it survives the rest.

The tree stays small when your moves are forcing. That is why a combination of checks can be calculated to the end, while a quiet position is judged instead.

sections.prompt: White to play. Petrosian–Spassky, World Championship 1966, game 10. Calculate to the end before you move.
sections.hint: The queen on g5 and the rook on f7 stand on squares a knight can reach with check.
sections.explanation: 30.Qh8+!! Kxh8 31.Nxf7+ forks the king and the queen. After 31...Kg7 32.Nxg5 White is a knight up. Spassky resigned after 30.Qh8+. The tree is tiny, because every white move is a check or a capture.

sections.caption: Botvinnik–Capablanca, AVRO 1938, after 30.Ba3!! Qxa3 31.Nh5+!. The tree is narrow: 31...gxh5 32.Qg5+ Kf8 33.Qxf6+ Kg8 34.e7 and the pawn decides; 31...Kh6 or 31...Kg8 lose the knight on f6, and 31...Kh8 or 31...Kf8 allow mate in two.

sections.prompt: White to play. Botvinnik–Capablanca, AVRO 1938. The pawn on e6 wants to run, and the queen on e7 stops it. Calculate the line that removes the queen.
sections.hint: Deflect the queen from e7. Which bishop move offers itself?
sections.explanation: 30.Ba3!! The game went 30...Qxa3 31.Nh5+! gxh5 32.Qg5+ Kf8 33.Qxf6+ Kg8 34.e7 and the pawn decided. If Black declines with 30...Qe8, then 31.Qc7+ Kg8 32.Be7 keeps a winning attack (engine about +4). Each branch ends in a position you can judge in one sentence.

sections.question: When do you stop calculating a line and judge the position?
options: When the position is quiet: no checks, captures or threats are left
After exactly three moves for each side
As soon as you find a check
When you have seen every legal move for both sides
sections.explanation: Stop where nothing is hanging and nobody has a forcing move. A position in the middle of an exchange cannot be judged: count the pieces only after the captures end.

lessons.title: Aagaard's three questions
lessons.objective: In a quiet position, find the move by asking where the weaknesses are, which piece is worst, and what the opponent wants.

sections.md:
Most moves in a game are not combinations. For quiet positions Aagaard trains three questions:

1. Where are the weaknesses? Pawns that no pawn can defend, holes, a weak king.
2. Which is my worst-placed piece? Find the piece that does least, and a route to a better square.
3. What does my opponent want to do? Name his plan or threat, and check whether your move can stop it.

These moves need little calculation. The answers point to a plan, and the plan names the move. Strong players save their time for the critical moments and play quiet moves like this quickly.

The model is Karpov's 24.Nb1!! against Spassky in 1974. The weaknesses were the black pawns on c6 and e5. The worst white piece was the knight on c3: it attacked nothing. So the knight went backwards, to b1 and d2, on its way to f3 and c4, where it hits e5 and c6.

sections.question: First question: which black pawns are the weaknesses?
options: c6 and e5
f7 and g6
g6 and h5
f7 and h5
sections.explanation: c6 has no neighbour on the b- or d-file, so no pawn can ever defend it, and it stands on the c-file in front of White's queen. e5 is fixed on a dark square in the centre. The kingside pawns are well protected.

sections.question: Second question: which white piece is worst placed?
options: The knight on c3
The queen on c4
The bishop on e3
The rook on f1
sections.explanation: The knight on c3 attacks no weakness: the pawn on c6 covers b5 and d5, and e4 holds White's own pawn. The queen hits c6 and f7, the bishop rules the dark squares, and the rook watches the half-open f-file. Karpov found the knight's route: 24.Nb1!, then d2 and f3. The engine rates 24.Nb1 as the best move.

sections.caption: Karpov–Spassky, Candidates 1974, White to move. The knight takes the long way: c3-b1-d2-f3, where it attacks e5. The pawns on c6 and e5 are the targets.

sections.question: Karpov played 24.Nb1. Which answer describes the plan?
options: The knight goes to d2 and then f3 or c4, where it attacks the weak pawn on e5
The knight defends the b2 pawn against the black knight
The knight makes room for the rook on c3
The knight retreats because it is attacked

lessons.title: Blumenfeld's rule: the last look
lessons.objective: After you finish calculating, look at the position once more as a beginner would, for checks, captures and loose pieces, before you touch a piece.

sections.md:
Kotov passes on a rule from Blumenfeld: after a long calculation, write your move on the scoresheet, then look at the board again with fresh eyes, as a beginner would. Is there a mate in one? Is something hanging? Can he check me?

Long calculation tires the eye. You see the deep line and miss the simple reply at move one. Many club games are lost exactly this way: the plan was right, the move was wrong.

The last look takes ten seconds:

1. After my move, what are all his checks?
2. What are all his captures?
3. Which of my pieces are loose, and is my back rank safe?

If the answer worries you, calculate again. If not, play the move.

In 1914 Bernstein won a pawn against Capablanca with 27.Nxc3. After 27...Nxc3 28.Rxc3 Rxc3 29.Rxc3 Qb2!! his back rank collapsed. One look at the first rank would have warned him.

sections.question: White is a knight down. 1.Rxd5 seems to win it back. Take the last look: should White play it?
options: No: 1...Qe1+ is mate, because the rook has left the first rank
Yes: the knight on d5 is loose
No: Black recaptures with 1...Qxd5
Yes: after 1.Rxd5 White is safe and level
sections.explanation: The rook on d1 is the only guard of the first rank. After 1.Rxd5 the queen comes to e1 with mate: f1 is covered by the queen, and the pawns on f2, g2 and h2 take the king's squares. The last look at Black's checks finds 1...Qe1 at once.

sections.question: Bernstein–Capablanca 1914. Bernstein played 27.Nxc3. What should his last look have found?
options: After 27...Nxc3 28.Rxc3 Rxc3 29.Rxc3 Qb2!! the queen on e2 cannot guard the first rank and the rook at the same time
27.Nxc3 is safe: White simply wins a pawn
27...Rxc3 wins the knight on the spot
Black has 27...Qxe3 with a fork
sections.explanation: The last look asks: where are my loose pieces, and is my back rank safe? White's king has no luft. After the exchanges on c3 both white rooks have left the first rank, the queen is its only guard, and the rook on c3 is loose: 29...Qb2!! hits both. Bernstein resigned.

sections.prompt: White to play. Capablanca–Tartakower, New York 1924. 37.Rxc7 wins a pawn. Take the last look first.
sections.hint: After 37.Rxc7, what are Black's checks and captures? Is there a better use of the tempo?
sections.explanation: 37.g6! builds a mating net: the rook on h7, the pawn on g6 and the king coming to g5 and f6. The game went 37...Rxf4+ 38.Kg5 Re4 39.Kf6 and White won. 37.Rxc7? Rxf4+ 38.Kh5 Rxd4 lets Black's rook and pawns loose, and the engine calls it equal. 37.Kh5 keeps an edge, but 37.g6 is the strongest.

modules.title: Rook endings and Shereshevsky's principles
modules.summary: Win rook against pawn and rook with two pawns, put the rook on the seventh, activate the king, and play the ending with Shereshevsky's principles.
modules.source: Steps Method Step 5 (rook against pawn, the seventh rank, rook endings); de la Villa, 100 Endgames You Must Know ch. 4 and 10 (rook v pawn, rook + two pawns v rook); Shereshevsky, Endgame Strategy (centralise the king, do not hurry, two weaknesses); Capablanca and Rubinstein rook endings

lessons.title: Rook against pawn
lessons.objective: Win with the rook against a lone pawn by cutting the enemy king off or attacking the pawn from behind.

sections.md:
Rook against pawn is the ending you reach after a race of passed pawns. The rook usually wins, but only if the defending king is kept away from its pawn.

Two techniques decide it:

1. Cut the king off. Put the rook on a rank or file between the enemy king and the pawn's path. A pawn without its king falls to the rook.
2. Attack the pawn from behind. A rook behind the pawn follows it all the way down and never loses time.

Then bring your own king. If your king reaches the pawn's path before the pawn reaches its last rank, you win.

The defender hopes for a pawn on the third or second rank, supported by its king, with your king far away. Then the best you get is the pawn for your rook, and the game is a draw.

In each position below exactly one rook move wins and every other move draws. The tablebase confirms it.

sections.prompt: White to play and win. Your king is far away.
sections.hint: Use the rook as a wall. Which rank stands between the black king and its pawn's path?
sections.explanation: 1.Rh5! cuts the king off along the fifth rank. The pawn must go on alone: 1...Ke6 2.Rc5 f3 3.Rc3 f2 4.Rf3 and it falls. Every other move draws, because the black king steps to e5 and e4 and escorts its pawn.

sections.prompt: White to play and win. The same idea on another file.
sections.hint: The black king must cross the fifth rank to support its pawn. Close that rank.
sections.explanation: 1.Rd5! The king on b6 is cut off from the c-pawn's path. 1...Kc6 2.Rf5 Kd6 3.Ke8 and the white king arrives in time. On 1.Rd1? Ka5 2.Rc1 Kb4 the king supports the pawn and White must give the rook for it: a draw.

sections.prompt: White to play and win. Where does the rook belong?
sections.hint: Get behind the pawn.
sections.explanation: 1.Rd2! attacks the pawn from behind. 1...d4 2.Rxd4+ wins it at once, and on 1...Ke5 2.Kg5 the white king joins in. The check 1.Rf2+? Ke3! only helps the king forward to its pawn: a draw.

sections.prompt: Win the pawn. Your rook already cuts the black king off along the fifth rank.
sections.tip: Keep the black king behind the fifth rank and bring your king. When the pawn advances, get your rook behind it.

sections.question: White to move. Which move wins?
options: 1.Rf5, cutting the king off along the fifth rank
1.Kf7, bringing the king
1.Rb2, stopping the pawn on its file
1.Rf4, attacking the pawn
sections.explanation: 1.Rf5! keeps the king on a6 away from b4, b3 and b2, and the pawn falls. 1.Rb2 stands in front of the pawn, and the black king comes to its aid; 1.Rf4 Kb5 and 1.Kf7 Kb5 also let the king through. The tablebase gives only 1.Rf5 as a win.

lessons.title: Rook and two pawns against rook
lessons.objective: Win with two connected pawns by protecting them before you push, and know the pairs of pawns that often draw.

sections.md:
Many won rook endings end as rook and two pawns against rook. De la Villa's rules:

1. Two connected passed pawns usually win. The defender cannot blockade both, and the pawns protect each other.
2. Protect the pawns before you push them. A pawn that runs ahead alone can be attacked by the enemy king and rook.
3. Cut the enemy king off with your rook, and keep your own king close to the pawns.
4. Not every pair wins. Doubled pawns are often worth little more than one pawn, and the f- and h-pawns together are a famous drawing case when the defending king stands in front of them.

The defender hopes for an active rook and king: checks from far away, and a king that reaches the squares in front of the pawns.

In both positions below one rook move wins. The natural alternatives let the win slip, and the engine calls them draws.

sections.prompt: White to play and win. The black king attacks f5.
sections.hint: Protect the pawns first. Where does your rook guard the f-pawn and stay out of the king's reach?
sections.explanation: 1.Rf2! guards the f-pawn from behind. Next comes f6 with the rook's support, and the white king walks up. The hasty 1.f6? Kf4! leaves the e5 pawn unprotected; the king attacks it and the engine calls the ending a draw.

sections.prompt: White to play and win. Your d-pawn is attacked.
sections.hint: A check first. Which rank must the black king not cross?
sections.explanation: 1.Rg7+! drives the king back. 1...Ke8 2.Rd7 and the rook shelters the d-pawn; 1...Kd6 2.Rd7+ Kc5 3.e7 and a pawn queens. 1.Re2? Rxd5+ gives a pawn away and the engine calls it a draw.

sections.prompt: Promote a pawn. Your rook guards the f-pawn from behind; the e-pawn still needs your king.
sections.tip: Bring the king up first: e2, f3, e4. Push a pawn only when it is protected, and answer rook checks by walking toward the pawns.

sections.question: Which pair of pawns gives the defender the best drawing chances in rook and two pawns against rook?
options: The f- and h-pawns
Connected e- and f-pawns
The c- and f-pawns
Connected d- and e-pawns on the sixth rank
sections.explanation: The f- and h-pawns are the classic drawing case: the defending king stands in front of them and the rook checks from behind or the side. Connected pawns, far-advanced pawns and pawns far apart are usually wins.

lessons.title: The seventh rank and the active king
lessons.objective: Put the rook on the seventh rank and bring the king forward: in rook endings, activity is often worth more than a pawn.

sections.md:
Rubinstein and Capablanca won their rook endings with two ideas.

The rook on the seventh rank. Most pawns still stand on their starting squares, so a rook on the seventh attacks them from the side. It also traps the enemy king on the back rank. It is often the best square for a rook in the endgame.

The active king. With queens off, the king is a fighting piece. It walks forward, supports its pawns and attacks the enemy pawns from the front.

Together they create mating threats even in a simple rook ending. A king on f6 or g6, a rook on the seventh and one pawn near the enemy king can be worth more than two extra pawns.

When you must choose between keeping a pawn and activating your rook or king, choose activity. A passive rook that guards a pawn ties down the whole army. A defender who gives a pawn to free his rook often saves the game; one who clings to the pawn often loses it.

lessons.title: Shereshevsky: centralise, do not hurry, two weaknesses
lessons.objective: In a better ending, centralise the king, create a second weakness, and improve every piece before you push.

sections.md:
Shereshevsky's book Endgame Strategy rests on five lessons:

1. Centralise the king. In the ending it is a strong piece. Use it first.
2. Do not hurry. If the opponent has no counterplay, improve every piece before you act. Each improvement is free.
3. The principle of two weaknesses. One weakness can be defended. Attack a second one on the other wing, and the defence breaks.
4. Exchange the right pieces. Trade the defender's good pieces and keep your own active ones.
5. Think in schemes. Picture the ideal set-up for your pieces, then find the moves that reach it.

Rubinstein's win against Cohn in 1909 shows the first two. With queens gone at move four, he centralised his king, traded into a pawn ending he had counted, walked the king to h3 and only then advanced his pawns, with tempo.

Capablanca's tenth game against Lasker in 1921 shows the third: the isolated pawn on d4 was weakness one, the pawn on b3 weakness two.

modules.title: Minor-piece endings: the de la Villa canon
modules.summary: Knight against pawn, bishops of the same and of opposite colours, and bishop against knight: the exact rules and the model game.
modules.source: de la Villa, 100 Endgames You Must Know ch. 2, 6, 7 and 8 (knight v pawn; bishop and pawn v bishop; bishop v knight; opposite-coloured bishops); Capablanca, Chess Fundamentals (knight v bishop); Fischer–Taimanov 1971

lessons.title: Knight against pawn
lessons.objective: Stop a passed pawn with the knight by reaching a square on its path with tempo, and know why the rook's pawn is the knight's worst enemy.

sections.md:
A knight is slow, but it can stop a pawn on its own if it reaches the pawn's path in time. De la Villa's rules for knight against pawn:

1. A knight on a square in front of the pawn holds it. The pawn can never pass a blockading knight.
2. If the knight cannot reach the path, it can attack the queening square instead. A knight that covers that square stops the pawn just as well.
3. Checks gain tempi. A knight check on the king often brings the knight one move closer for free.
4. Watch for the fork. If the pawn queens on a square the knight can check from, the new queen may be lost at once.
5. The rook's pawn is the knight's worst enemy. In the corner the knight has few squares, and a rook's pawn on the seventh rank, supported by its king, can be impossible to stop.

In the three challenges below, exactly one knight move saves the game; every other move lets the pawn queen. The tablebase confirms each one.

sections.caption: The knight on b1 blockades the pawn on b2, and the white king is close enough to help. The tablebase gives a draw.

sections.prompt: White to play and draw. The pawn is one step from c1.
sections.hint: The knight needs one tempo more than it has. Find a check that also brings it closer.
sections.explanation: 1.Nd4+! The check gains the tempo. After the king moves, the knight reaches b3 or e2, from where it covers c1, or simply takes on c2. Every other move loses: the pawn queens.

sections.hint: Head for c3 or e3. What happens if Black queens at once?
sections.explanation: 1.Nd5! If 1...d1=Q, 2.Nc3+ forks king and queen. If 1...Kc2, then 2.Ne3+ and 3.Nd1 blockades the pawn. Any other knight move is too slow.

options: A rook's pawn on the seventh rank, supported by its king
A centre pawn on the fifth rank
A knight's pawn on the fourth rank
A pawn that is still on its starting square
sections.explanation: Near the corner the knight has very few squares. Against a rook's pawn on the seventh with its king nearby, the knight often cannot reach a square in front of the pawn or cover the queening square in time.

lessons.title: Bishops of the same colour
lessons.objective: Hold bishop and pawn against bishop with the king in front of the pawn, and win it by blocking the defending bishop's diagonal.

sections.md:
Bishop and pawn against bishop of the same colour is a common ending, and its rules are simple.

The defender draws if his king stands in front of the pawn on a square of the colour the attacking bishop cannot reach. The bishop can never drive the king away, and the king alone is enough.

When the defending king is cut off, the defending bishop must stop the pawn alone. It does this from a diagonal that crosses the pawn's path. The attacker then wins by interference: he puts his own bishop on that diagonal, between the defending bishop and the square it guards. The defender must either exchange bishops, and the pawn queens, or leave the diagonal, and the pawn advances.

So the defender's rule is: king in front. The attacker's rule is: cut the enemy king off, then block the diagonal.

Shorter diagonals are easier to block. Count the squares of each diagonal that crosses the pawn's path before you decide where your bishop goes.

sections.caption: A draw. The black king stands on e6, a light square, in front of the pawn. White's dark-squared bishop can never attack it, and the engine gives 0.00.

options: Black's king stands in front of the pawn on a square White's bishop cannot attack
Bishops of the same colour always draw
Black's bishop attacks the pawn
White's king is too far away from the pawn
sections.explanation: With the king on e6, a light square, White's dark-squared bishop can never drive it off, and the pawn cannot pass it. Bishops of the same colour do not always draw: when the defending king is cut off, interference wins, as in the two challenges.

lessons.title: Opposite-coloured bishops
lessons.objective: Know when opposite-coloured bishops draw (one extra pawn, a blockade on the right colour) and when they win (pawns far apart, or an attack in the middlegame).

sections.md:
With opposite-coloured bishops each bishop rules its own colour and can never fight the other one. That gives the endings their character.

1. One extra pawn is almost always a draw. The defender puts his king or bishop in front of the pawn on his bishop's colour, or gives the bishop for the pawn.
2. With two extra pawns, the defender blocks with the king on the colour the enemy bishop cannot attack, and stops the other pawn with his bishop.
3. Pawns far apart usually win. The king cannot block one pawn and the bishop guard the other at the same time when they are on opposite wings.
4. In the middlegame, opposite-coloured bishops favour the attacker. The defending bishop cannot cover the squares of the other colour around its king.

When you defend, put your king on the squares the enemy bishop cannot reach. When you attack, make passed pawns as far apart as you can.

sections.prompt: White to play and win. Your pawns stand on opposite wings.
sections.hint: Make the bishop or king commit to the g-pawn, then run with the a-pawn.
sections.explanation: 1.g7! Black must stop the g-pawn with the king (1...Kf7 2.Bd4) or with the bishop (1...Bh7). Then the a-pawn runs with the white king beside it, and Black has nothing left to stop it. 1.Bd4? Bxg6 gives up the g-pawn: a draw.

sections.question: White has a bishop and one extra pawn; Black's bishop is of the opposite colour. What is the usual result?
options: A draw
A win for White
A win for Black
It depends only on whose move it is
sections.explanation: One extra pawn with opposite-coloured bishops is almost always a draw: the defender puts his king or bishop in front of the pawn on his own colour, or gives the bishop for the last pawn.

lessons.title: Bishop against knight
lessons.objective: Use the bishop's range against a knight when pawns stand on both wings, and dominate a knight on the rim.

sections.md:
Bishop or knight? Capablanca's answer: the bishop is usually better in an open position with pawns on both wings, and the knight is better in a closed position or on a protected outpost.

The bishop's strength is range. From one square it watches both wings, and it can wait: a bishop can make a waiting move along its diagonal without losing anything, which matters in zugzwang. The knight is slow; it needs several moves to cross the board.

A knight on the rim is weakest. On the edge it has at most four squares, and a bishop can sometimes cover all of them at once. Then the knight is dominated: it cannot move, and the king comes to take it, or a pawn runs past it.

Fischer against Taimanov in 1971 is the model game. Pawns on both wings, a bishop that kept gaining tempi, and a king that walked to a6. In the end Fischer gave the bishop for one pawn, because two connected passed pawns beat the knight.

modules.title: Strategy II: Silman's imbalances
modules.summary: List the imbalances for both sides, then play for the superior minor piece, the key file and space, and use dynamic advantages before they fade.
modules.source: Silman, How to Reassess Your Chess (4th ed.): the ten imbalances and the thinking technique; Steps Method Step 5 (material and time); model games Botvinnik–Capablanca 1938, Karpov–Kasparov 1984 and 1985, Karpov–Unzicker 1974

lessons.title: The ten imbalances
lessons.objective: List the imbalances for both sides before you choose a plan, and play where your imbalances point.

sections.md:
Silman's method starts with a list, not a move. An imbalance is any difference between the two sides. How to Reassess Your Chess names ten:

1. Superior minor piece (bishop against knight, good bishop against bad).
2. Pawn structure: doubled, isolated, backward or passed pawns, majorities.
3. Space.
4. Material.
5. Control of a key file.
6. Control of a hole or weak square.
7. Lead in development.
8. Initiative.
9. King safety.
10. Statics against dynamics: is your plus permanent, or must you use it now?

The thinking technique has five steps. List the imbalances for both sides. Decide which ones favour you and on which side of the board they point. Picture your dream position. Only then look for candidate moves that move toward it. Finally, calculate and check the tactics.

Strong players often see a move first and justify it afterwards. That is fine: use the list to test the move you already like.

sections.caption: Botvinnik–Capablanca, AVRO 1938, White to move. Material: Black is a pawn up. Pawn structure: White has a mobile centre (d4, e4, f3), Black a queenside majority. Minor pieces: the bishop on b2 is shut in by its own pawns. King safety: Black's queen and the knight on b3 are far from their king.

sections.question: Which imbalance gives White his plan here?
options: The mobile central pawns, which can advance with e5 and f4-f5 toward Black's king
Material: White is a pawn up
The bishop on b2, which controls the long diagonal
The queenside pawn majority
sections.explanation: Black is the one who is a pawn up, and the queenside majority is Black's too. The bishop on b2 is blocked by c3 and d4. White's trump is the centre: Botvinnik played 20.e5, 22.f4 and 24.f5 and won with an attack.

sections.question: In Silman's thinking technique, what comes right after you list the imbalances?
options: Decide which imbalances favour you and on which side of the board to play
Calculate every forcing line
Play the most natural developing move
Offer to exchange queens
sections.explanation: The order is: list the imbalances, choose the ones that favour you and the side of the board, picture the dream position, then find candidate moves, then calculate. Calculation comes last, when you know what you are calculating for.

sections.question: Black's extra pawn is a static plus; White's mobile centre and attacking chances are dynamic. What does that mean for White?
options: White must act quickly, before Black consolidates and the extra pawn starts to count
White can wait: dynamic advantages last forever
White should exchange queens at once
White should play on the queenside, where Black is strong
sections.explanation: A static plus (material, structure) lasts. A dynamic plus (development, initiative, an attack) fades if it is not used. The side with the dynamic plus must play energetically; the side with the static plus wants to calm the game down.

lessons.title: Superior minor piece: knight against bad bishop
lessons.objective: Recognise a bad bishop (blocked by its own pawns on its colour) and a good knight, and trade into the ending where the difference decides.

sections.md:
A bishop is bad when its own centre pawns stand on its colour. The pawns block its diagonals, and the squares of the other colour become holes that the bishop can never cover. A knight, on the other hand, attacks squares of both colours.

Silman calls it the superior minor piece. It is a static imbalance: it lasts as long as the pawns stay where they are. So the side with the good piece wants exchanges of everything else, and the side with the bad bishop wants to change the pawn structure or keep the game dynamic.

The test is simple. Count the pawns on your bishop's colour, especially the centre pawns that cannot move. Then ask where the enemy knight wants to go: a square in front of a blocked pawn, which no pawn can attack, is ideal.

Karpov against Kasparov, 1984, is the model. Black's isolated d5 pawn stood on a light square, his remaining pawns followed it onto light squares, and the light-squared bishop on e6 had nothing to do. White's knight attacked from b4.

sections.question: Black to move. Why is the bishop on e6 a bad bishop?
options: All six black pawns stand on light squares, the bishop's own colour
It is pinned to the king
It is attacked by the knight on c3
It has no legal moves
sections.explanation: a6, b5, d5, f7, g6 and h5 are all light squares. The bishop must defend them and can never attack White's pawns on dark squares. The knight on c3 attacks squares of both colours.

lessons.title: Files and space: Karpov's squeeze
lessons.objective: Take the only open file, use extra space to restrict the enemy pieces, and squeeze until the opponent runs out of useful moves.

sections.md:
Two of Silman's imbalances often work together: control of a key file and space.

A file is key when it is the only open one. Whoever controls it can bring rooks to the seventh or eighth rank, and the other side's rooks have nowhere to go. Control means more than one rook on it, or a piece that stops the opponent from contesting it.

Space is the territory behind your pawn chain. With more space your pieces can move from one wing to the other; the cramped side's pieces get in each other's way.

The method against a cramped opponent is the squeeze:

1. Close the centre so that he has no counterplay there.
2. Take the open file.
3. Improve every piece slowly. He has no good moves, so time is on your side.
4. Open a second front only when his pieces are tied up.

Karpov against Unzicker, 1974, is the classic. The a-file was the only open file, and Karpov's 24.Ba7!! made sure Black could never contest it.

sections.question: Why did Karpov put his bishop on a7?
options: To block the a-file: Black can never contest it, while White doubles rooks behind the bishop
To attack the black king
To win the pawn on d6
To defend the pawn on b4
sections.explanation: From a7 the bishop cuts the a-file in two. White's rooks gather behind it on a2 and a1, and Black's rook on a8 cannot challenge them. The bishop attacks neither d6 nor the king, and it does not defend b4.

lessons.title: Statics against dynamics: material and time
lessons.objective: Decide whether to grab material or play for time and activity, and use a dynamic advantage before it fades.

sections.md:
The Steps Method calls it material and time; Silman calls it statics against dynamics. A pawn is a static asset: it stays. A lead in development or an active piece is a dynamic asset: if you do not use it, it disappears.

So the questions are:

1. Can I take the material safely, or does it cost me time my opponent will use?
2. If I am the one with the dynamic plus, can I turn it into something static before it fades: a pawn, a weakness, an outpost?
3. If I have the static plus, can I survive the next few moves and then consolidate?

An old rule of thumb: three tempi of development are worth about a pawn. Do not grab a pawn when your king is in the centre and his pieces are already out.

The best dynamic gains are lasting ones. In 1985 Kasparov gave a pawn for a knight on d3 that no white pawn could ever attack. In 1938 Botvinnik gave the a-pawn for a mobile centre and an attack.

sections.question: Kasparov is a pawn down. What did he get for it?

sections.explanation: White has no c- or e-pawn left to chase the knight from d3. From there it hits b2, c1, e1 and f2 and cuts White's position in two. Both sides have two bishops, so the bishop pair is not the answer.

lessons.title: The pawn chain: attack the base
lessons.objective: Find the pawn chains, attack the enemy chain at its base with a pawn break, and play on the side your own chain points to.

sections.md:
A pawn chain is a diagonal line of pawns, each one protecting the next. In the French Defence after 1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.e5, White's chain runs d4-e5 and Black's runs e6-d5.

Nimzowitsch's rules for chains:

1. Attack the chain at its base, the rearmost pawn, because nothing protects it. If the base falls, the whole chain is weak.
2. The head of the chain, the most advanced pawn, can also be attacked, but it is protected and the attack is usually slower.
3. Play on the side of the board your chain points to. White's chain d4-e5 points to the kingside, so White attacks there; Black's chain points to the queenside, so Black plays ...c5 and puts pressure on d4.

In the French, Black's breaks are ...c5 against d4 and ...f6 against e5. White's breaks are f4-f5 against e6 and, less often, c4 against d5.

Nimzowitsch added a twist: you can also give up the base and hold the square with pieces instead. That leads to the blockade, the next lesson.

sections.question: Black's ...c5 attacks the base of White's chain. Which other pawn break attacks the chain, this time at its head?
sections.explanation: ...f6 hits e5, the head of the chain d4-e5. Salwe played it on move 8. ...b5, ...g5 and ...a5 do not touch White's pawns at all.

sections.question: Which white pawn break attacks the base of Black's chain e6-d5?
options: f4-f5
c3-c4
b2-b4
h2-h4
sections.explanation: The base of Black's chain is e6, and f4-f5 attacks it. c3-c4 would hit the head, d5. b2-b4 and h2-h4 gain space but attack no pawn of the chain.

sections.question: Nimzowitsch now played 7.dxc5!? and gave up the base of his own chain. What was the idea?
options: To hold d4 and e5 with pieces instead of pawns, so that they cannot be attacked by Black's pawns
To win the c5 pawn and keep it
To open the c-file for his rook
To castle queenside
sections.explanation: After 7...Bxc5 White does not keep the pawn. The point, in My System, is that a piece on d4 cannot be chased away by ...c5 any more, and that e5 is then held by pieces too. This is the blockade.

lessons.title: Blockade and overprotection
lessons.objective: Stop an enemy pawn with a piece on the square in front of it, and overprotect your key squares so that their defenders become strong.

sections.md:
Nimzowitsch's law for passed and isolated pawns: first restrain, then blockade, finally destroy.

The blockade is a piece on the square directly in front of the enemy pawn. The pawn cannot move, so it can no longer support an attack or threaten to promote. The blockading piece is hard to drive away. In front of an isolated pawn it is completely safe, because the pawn has no neighbours that could attack it. The best blockader is a knight: it keeps attacking even while it blocks.

Overprotection is the other half of the idea. When a square is important, such as an outpost or the square in front of a blockaded pawn, defend it more times than it is attacked. The pieces that overprotect it are not passive: they stand on good squares, and when the moment comes they can attack from there.

In Nimzowitsch–Salwe, 1911, White gave up his d4 pawn on move 7, put a bishop on d4 in front of Black's d5 pawn, and guarded e5 with knight, bishop and later rooks. Black's centre pawns stayed frozen until White's attack had begun.

sections.question: Which white piece is the blockader?
options: The bishop on d4
The queen on e2
The rook on e1
The bishop on d3
sections.explanation: The bishop on d4 stands directly in front of Black's d5 pawn, so the pawn cannot move. The queen and the rook support it; the bishop on d3 aims at the king.

lessons.title: Open files and the seventh rank
lessons.objective: Take the open file with a rook, use it to reach the seventh rank, and keep your king central when the queens are off.

sections.md:
Nimzowitsch's elements of rook play:

1. An open file is a road. A rook on it is not the goal; the goal is the entry square at the end of the road, usually on the seventh or eighth rank.
2. Take the file first and double rooks on it if the opponent contests it.
3. The seventh rank is the target. There the rook attacks pawns from the side and shuts the enemy king in. Two rooks on the seventh are often decisive on their own.
4. If the entry squares are guarded, prepare them: exchange the guard, or attack it with a minor piece.

A practical rule for the ending: with queens off, put the king in the centre first, then use the file. A rook on the seventh and an active king together win most endings.

Rubinstein against Schlechter, 1912, shows the whole plan: queens off on move eleven, the king on e3, the rook on c7, and a pawn storm while Black's pieces were tied to the seventh rank.

sections.question: Rubinstein played 16.Rc7. What makes c7 a good square for the rook?
options: It is on the seventh rank, at the end of the open c-file: the rook attacks the bishop on c8 and the pawn on f7
It attacks the black king directly
It defends White's d-pawn
It traps the black knight on b8
sections.explanation: The c-file is open, and c7 is its entry square on the seventh rank. From there the rook attacks the bishop on c8 and the pawn on f7, and Black's pieces must defend instead of developing. The rook does not defend d4 or trap the knight.

lessons.title: Exchanging and the exchange sacrifice
lessons.objective: Judge an exchange by the position that remains, and give the exchange when it buys a lasting positional asset.

sections.md:
Nimzowitsch treats exchanging as an element of its own. An exchange is good or bad only because of what stays on the board. Three typical reasons to exchange:

1. Remove the opponent's best piece, or the defender of a key square.
2. Win time: exchange a piece that has just developed, so the opponent must spend a move recapturing.
3. Change the position into one where your remaining pieces are better.

Fischer's 22.Nxd7+ against Petrosian in 1971 is the model of the third. He gave his strong knight for a bad bishop, because after the exchange White's rooks owned the c-file and the seventh rank.

Petrosian made the same judgement in reverse with the exchange sacrifice. A rook is worth more than a minor piece only if it has open lines. When a knight gets an unbreakable square, and the rook would have no files, a minor piece and a lasting bind can be worth more than the rook.

sections.question: Fischer played 22.Nxd7+, giving his fine knight for Black's bad bishop. Why?
options: After 22...Rxd7 23.Rc1 White owns the c-file and the seventh rank, and Black's knight cannot match the bishop
The knight was attacked and had to move
It wins material by force
To avoid a draw by repetition
sections.explanation: Nothing attacked the knight, and no material changes hands. The point is what remains: White's rooks enter on c7 and the seventh rank, and Black's pieces are passive. Fischer won in twelve more moves.

lessons.title: Prophylaxis and restraint
lessons.objective: Before you follow your own plan, find your opponent's plan and stop it, especially his pawn breaks.

sections.md:
Prophylaxis means prevention: a move that stops the opponent's plan before it starts. Nimzowitsch made it a method; Dvoretsky later turned it into a habit with one question: what does my opponent want to do?

The steps:

1. Imagine it is his move. What would he play? Name the threat or the plan: a pawn break, a knight jump, a rook lift.
2. Ask whether your next move can stop it, or make it bad.
3. Only then continue your own plan.

Pawn breaks are the most important target. A cramped position frees itself with a pawn break; if you restrain the break, the opponent has no plan at all. Nimzowitsch's order is restrain, blockade, destroy.

The famous example is Johner–Nimzowitsch, Dresden 1926. White's only active plan was g2-g4, followed by f4-f5. Nimzowitsch played ...h5 and then took his queen to h7. From there it watches f5, and if White ever plays g4, the h-file opens toward the white king with the black queen already on it.

sections.question: Black to move. What does White want to play?
options: g2-g4, followed by f4-f5, to open lines on the kingside

sections.question: Why does 16...Qh7 stop White's g2-g4?
options: After g4 hxg4 hxg4 the h-file opens toward the king on h2, with the black queen already on it
The queen attacks g4 directly
The queen pins the g2 pawn
The queen protects the e4 pawn

modules.title: A repertoire through structures: the Queen's Gambit family
modules.summary: Learn the Queen's Gambit and Nimzo-Indian through their pawn structures: the Carlsbad minority attack, the isolated queen's pawn, hanging pawns and the central majority, each with a model game.
modules.source: Soltis, Pawn Structure Chess (the Queen's Gambit family: Carlsbad, isolani, hanging pawns; the Nimzo-Indian formation); Yusupov, Boost Your Chess 3 ch. 6 and 19 (hanging pawns, central pawn majority); model games Smyslov–Keres 1948, Botvinnik–Vidmar 1936, Bernstein–Capablanca 1914, Botvinnik–Capablanca 1938

lessons.title: The Carlsbad structure: the minority attack
lessons.objective: In the Queen's Gambit Exchange structure, attack Black's three queenside pawns with two, b4-b5, to leave a weak pawn on c6, or switch to the central plan f3 and e4.

sections.md:
A repertoire is easier to learn through its pawn structures than through long move lists. The Queen's Gambit Declined, Exchange Variation, 1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bg5 and cxd5 exd5, gives the Carlsbad structure: White pawns on a2, b2, d4 and e3 against Black pawns on a7, b7, c6 and d5.

White's main plan is the minority attack. Two pawns attack three: b2-b4 and b4-b5, then bxc6. Whatever Black does, he is left with a weak pawn: a backward c6 pawn on the half-open c-file, or an isolated d5 pawn. White's rook goes to b1 behind the b-pawn, and the knights aim at c5 and e5.

White's second plan is central: Nge2, f2-f3 and e3-e4, a pawn roller in the centre and an attack. Botvinnik used it against Keres in 1952.

Black's counterplay is on the kingside: knights on e4 and g6, the f-pawn to f5, sometimes ...h5-h4. Black must be quick, because the queenside weakness is permanent.

sections.question: Which plan fits this structure for White?
options: The minority attack: b4-b5 and bxc6, leaving Black a weak pawn on c6
Push the d-pawn to d5
Play c2-c4 to attack d5
Push a2-a4-a5 to win the a7 pawn
sections.explanation: White has no c-pawn left, and d5 is blocked by Black's pawn, so the queenside pawn break is b4-b5. After bxc6 Black must accept a weak pawn on c6 or an isolated one on d5.

Because f3 was attacked by a black pawn

lessons.title: The isolated queen's pawn
lessons.objective: With the isolated pawn, attack on the kingside and prepare d4-d5; against it, blockade d5 and exchange pieces.

sections.md:
The isolated queen's pawn (IQP) is a d-pawn with no pawns on the c- and e-files beside it. It comes from many openings: the Queen's Gambit Accepted, the Tarrasch Defence, the Panov Attack against the Caro-Kann, the Semi-Tarrasch.

For the side with the IQP, the pawn is a strength in the middlegame. It controls e5 and c5, the open c- and e-files belong to the rooks, and the pieces are active. The plan is an attack: a knight on e5, the queen and bishop aimed at h7, a rook lift, the f-pawn to f4 and f5. The other big idea is the break d4-d5, which opens lines just when the opponent's pieces are not ready.

For the defender, the pawn is a weakness in the ending. The plan is the opposite: blockade the square in front of it, d5, with a knight, and exchange pieces. Every exchange takes away attacking force and brings the ending closer, where the pawn is simply weak.

So the question in every IQP position is timing: attack now, or trade down.

lessons.title: Hanging pawns
lessons.objective: Use hanging pawns as a mobile centre that advances at the right moment, and against them, force an advance that fixes them.

sections.md:
Hanging pawns are two pawns side by side, usually on c5 and d5 (or c4 and d4), with no pawns of their own colour on the files next to them. They arise in the Queen's Gambit Declined, the Tarrasch and many Queen's Indian lines.

They are strong and weak at the same time. Strong, because they control the centre and can advance: ...d4 or ...c4 opens lines or creates a passed pawn. Weak, because no pawn can protect them; if one advances at the wrong moment, the other is left behind and the square in front of the first becomes a hole.

For the side with the pawns: keep them side by side, use the half-open b- and e-files, and push one of them when the pieces are ready.

For the opponent: attack them with pieces on the c- and d-files, and provoke an advance. Once one pawn has moved, blockade it and attack the one left behind.

Capablanca turned his hanging pawns into a passed c-pawn against Bernstein in 1914. Fischer forced Spassky's pawns forward in 1972 and fixed them.

options: To force an advance (Spassky played 20...d4), after which the pawns are fixed and e6 is weak
To exchange queens
To open the long diagonal for his dark-squared bishop
To prepare castling

lessons.title: Nimzo-Indian: doubled pawns and the central majority
lessons.objective: With the doubled c-pawns and the bishop pair, build a central pawn majority and roll it forward; let a flank pawn go if the centre gains time.

sections.md:
The Nimzo-Indian, 1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4, often reaches a structure where Black takes on c3 and White has doubled c-pawns. Each side gets something.

White gets the bishop pair, an open b-file, and pawns that can build a broad centre: with Ne2, f2-f3 and e3-e4, the central majority rolls forward toward the black king.

Black gets a target: the doubled c-pawns, especially c4, attacked by ...c5, ...b6, ...Ba6 and ...Na5. Black also tries to close the centre, so that White's bishops have no open diagonals. Johner–Nimzowitsch, 1926, shows Black's plan: blockade and restraint.

Botvinnik–Capablanca, AVRO 1938, shows White's plan at its best. Capablanca closed the queenside with ...c4 and won the a-pawn. Botvinnik let it go: e3-e4-e5 and f2-f3-f4-f5 brought the pawns to the black king, and 26.Re6 and 30.Ba3 decided. A mobile central majority is worth more than a flank pawn.

sections.question: Black has just played 5...Bxc3+ 6.bxc3. What did Black give up for White's doubled c-pawns?
options: The bishop pair
A pawn
The right to castle
Control of the e-file
sections.explanation: Black's dark-squared bishop is gone, so White has two bishops against bishop and knight. Material is level and Black can still castle. That trade, bishop pair for structure, is the main imbalance of the Nimzo-Indian.
